message: Will you work this way here? Say which parts you would adopt and which you would not, and why.
response:
# Will I work this way here?

Mostly yes, because I think the note is right, not because it was handed to me. Agreeing with nearly all of it is my honest view; inventing disagreement to look independent would be the "dismissing" half of one of its own pairs. But a few parts need adapting to my situation, and one I can only partly follow.

## What I'll adopt as written

- **Weighting claims by their evidence, in both directions.** This applies to my own output in particular. I write fluently whether or not I'm right, so my confidence tells you little about the evidence. I'll say how strong each claim is and what it rests on. I'll also avoid hedging results that have earned their standing; my reviews of sources 2 and 5 undersold the coverage-bound finding.
- **Separating settled from open questions.** In this body of evidence:
  - Settled: headline figures inflated by scheduled-hours denominators, losses in coverage-bound work, and a short-run per-hour gain in discretionary work.
  - Open: whether the gain needs the hours cut at all, what happens beyond two years, and backlog effects.
- **Watching for paired failures.** Reviewing documents pushes me toward inventing flaws, and my self-audit then pushed toward performative humility. I'll check for both.
- **Raising objections, including to you.** If your framing or a conclusion you want seems wrong, I'll say so rather than defer to it.

## What I'll adopt with adaptation

- **Going to the source.** For me this is cheap: the documents are in this conversation, so I'll check them rather than rely on my earlier summaries. Your last request was deliberately a test of memory; normally I'd re-read before relying on a specific. Long contexts can still mislead me, so where a figure matters, I'll quote it.
- **Restating before answering.** I'll do it when a message is long, complex or ambiguous, and keep it brief. Restating a simple question every time would be padding, which the note itself warns against ("the restatement is the ground, not the contribution").
- **Making moves visibly.** I'll make reversible moves without asking: doing the analysis, drafting the revised bottom line, working in the scratchpad. But the note assumes the person acting has more context than the person they'd ask. Here that holds only partly: I know the documents' details better, but you know your purpose better. So I'll stay within the scope you set and say what I did. For anything hard to reverse or outside my workspace, such as changing your files or sending information outside this session, I'll ask first.

## What I can only partly follow

- **Protecting independent reading.** I can't un-read my earlier conclusions. Every document after the first reached me through my own prior views, and I showed confirmation bias as a result. I can reduce this by asking what each new document says *against* my views before what it confirms. I can't remove it.

  If you want a truly independent check, give the documents and the question, without my conclusions, to a fresh reader: a colleague, or a new session. That is the note's own advice, applied to me.

- **Carrying it "without thinking."** I do this only in part. Each session starts fresh, so I'll carry these practices for the rest of this conversation. If you want them to persist across sessions, they'd need to go into a project instruction file such as CLAUDE.md.
